title: Senior's toolkit: debugging functions and modules
summary: Attach a real debugger to Node, find who called a function, and fix the module errors everyone hits.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: debugging functions and modules
steps.body: Closures, `this` and imports go wrong in ways that are hard to see from the code alone. Experienced developers stop the program and look, using these tools.

toolkit.what: Start Node with the debugger port open and pause on the first line. Open `chrome://inspect` in Chrome (or attach VS Code) to set breakpoints and look at every variable in every closure.
flags: open the debugger port (127.0.0.1:9229) and keep running
open the port and pause before the first line
wait for a debugger to attach, then run (Node 22.2+)
toolkit.when: a script misbehaves and you want to step through it

toolkit.what: In VS Code, run **Debug: JavaScript Debug Terminal** from the command palette. Any `node`, `npm run` or `npx vitest` started in it has the debugger attached, with no launch.json.
flags: conditional breakpoint or logpoint (logs without editing code)
toolkit.example: npm run dev   # in the Debug Terminal: breakpoints just work

toolkit.what: A statement that pauses execution right there when a debugger is attached, and does nothing otherwise. Handy inside a callback that is hard to reach with a breakpoint.
Print a stack trace from where it is called: the quickest answer to "who is calling this function with a bad value?"
flags: printed first, so you can find it in the noise
the same trace as a string, to log or attach

toolkit.what: In package.json, makes `.js` and `.ts` files ES modules, so `import`/`export` work and files run in strict mode. Without it, Node treats them as CommonJS.
flags: force one file to ESM or CommonJS

toolkit.what: Import something that exists only as a type. It is erased completely, so Node never looks for a runtime export that is not there.
flags: the whole import is types only
mix a type and a value in one import
tsconfig option that makes `tsc` insist on this

steps.prompt: `node src/main.ts` stops at once with this. `types.ts` contains `export interface Order { ... }`. What is the fix?
code: SyntaxError: The requested module './types.ts' does not provide an export named 'Order'
options: Write `import type { Order } from "./types.ts"`: an interface is erased, so at run time there is no `Order` export
Change `interface` to `class` so it is exported
Remove the `.ts` extension from the import
steps.explain: Node strips types file by file, so it cannot know `Order` was only a type. `import type` (or `import { type Order }`) tells it to drop the import. Turn on `verbatimModuleSyntax` so `tsc` flags this before Node does.

steps.prompt: A classic interview question, and a real bug in old code. What does this print?
code: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
steps.explain: `var` is function-scoped, so all three closures capture the same `i`, which is 3 when they run. With `let` each iteration gets its own binding and it prints `0,1,2`. A breakpoint inside the arrow shows the shared variable in the Closure scope.

steps.prompt: In a class `Counter`, `setTimeout(counter.tick, 100)` crashes with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'count')`. Which change fixes it?
options: `setTimeout(() => counter.tick(), 100)`: the method must be called on `counter`, so `this` is set
Make `count` a `var` instead of a field
steps.explain: Passing `counter.tick` passes the bare function; when the timer calls it, `this` is `undefined` (class code is strict). An arrow wrapper or `counter.tick.bind(counter)` keeps `this`. The second option calls `tick` immediately and passes its result.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the situation.
pairs: pause a script before its first line and step through
debug `npm run dev` without writing a launch config
see which code called a function
pause inside a callback when a debugger is attached
import an interface without a runtime export

steps.prompt: Pause a script before it runs any code, then attach from Chrome.
steps.explain: `--inspect-brk` opens the debugger port and pauses on line one. Plain `--inspect` opens the port but keeps running, so a short script is finished before you attach. `about:debugging` is Firefox's page.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When a closure or `this` surprises you, stop guessing and set a breakpoint: the Scope panel shows exactly which variables a function captured. Keep a JavaScript Debug Terminal open in VS Code, so debugging any script or test is just running it.
